blocks.text: A first-time mother has been pushing for two and a half hours. The fetal heart rate, steady until now, drops to 70 beats per minute with each contraction and is slow to recover. The head is visible but has not advanced for 30 minutes. The midwife presses the emergency bell. Should the team wait, pull with an instrument, or go to theatre? Abnormal labour is largely about recognising which of these is safe, and how soon.

blocks.markdown: Normal labour needs three things to work together, often called the **three Ps**: the **Powers** (effective uterine contractions and maternal effort), the **Passage** (the bony pelvis and soft tissues) and the **Passenger** (fetal size, presentation, position and attitude). **Dystocia**, or failure to progress, is slow or arrested labour, and almost always results from a problem in one of these three.

blocks.title: Delay in labour (UK guidance)
blocks.text: NICE defines the established first stage as regular painful contractions with cervical dilatation of 4 cm or more. Delay in the established first stage is suspected when dilatation is less than 2 cm in 4 hours, or when there is slowing of progress, including descent and rotation of the head. In the second stage, delay is suspected in a nulliparous woman when active second stage has lasted 2 hours without birth imminent (1 hour in a parous woman). Thresholds vary between guidelines and units.

rows: Inefficient uterine contractions, exhaustion, poor effort with epidural
Amniotomy if membranes intact, then oxytocin infusion after assessment
Cephalopelvic disproportion, contracted pelvis, fibroids, full bladder
Empty bladder, reassess; caesarean section if obstruction is confirmed
Occipito-posterior or occipito-transverse position, deflexed head, macrosomia, brow or face presentation
Assess position, encourage upright and mobile positions; consider rotation or caesarean section
blocks.caption: Common causes of failure to progress.

blocks.markdown: When labour is slow, the assessment asks first whether the **powers** are inadequate, because that is the correctable cause. Review contraction frequency (adequate labour has about four to five contractions per 10 minutes), the position of the head, caput and moulding, and any signs of obstruction. Intervention is not triggered by time alone: it is triggered by delay together with a reassessment of maternal and fetal condition. If the powers are weak and there is no obstruction, **amniotomy** (artificial rupture of the membranes) and then an **oxytocin infusion** are used, with a vaginal examination 4 hours later to reassess.

blocks.title: Calculating an oxytocin infusion rate
blocks.prompt: Oxytocin 10 units is made up in 500 mL of crystalloid. The infusion pump runs at 24 mL per hour. How many milliunits per minute (mU/min) is the woman receiving? (Teaching example only; local protocols determine concentration and titration.)

steps.text: Convert the dose to milliunits and find the concentration.
Multiply by the pump rate to get milliunits per hour.

blocks.markdown: **Instrumental delivery** shortens the second stage using forceps or a vacuum extractor (ventouse). Indications are **fetal compromise**, **delay in the second stage**, **maternal exhaustion** and a **maternal medical reason to limit pushing** (for example significant cardiac disease). It requires strict **prerequisites**: cervix fully dilated, membranes ruptured, head engaged (no more than one-fifth palpable abdominally) with a known position, an empty bladder, adequate analgesia, informed consent and the ability to proceed to caesarean section if the attempt fails. The ventouse is avoided before 34 weeks (contraindicated below 32 weeks) and in face presentation. Forceps give a higher success rate and are used when rotation or a flexed head is not an issue, but carry more risk of perineal injury; the ventouse carries more risk of cephalohaematoma and retinal haemorrhage.

**Caesarean section** is performed when vaginal birth is unsafe or impossible. Indications include fetal compromise, failure to progress, obstruction, placenta praevia, malpresentation such as breech or transverse lie, and previous uterine rupture. The UK classifies urgency in four categories. **Category 1**: immediate threat to the life of the woman or fetus (aim for delivery within 30 minutes of the decision). **Category 2**: maternal or fetal compromise that is not immediately life-threatening (aim for delivery within about 75 minutes). **Category 3**: early delivery needed without compromise. **Category 4**: delivery timed to suit the woman and the service (elective).

blocks.title: Choosing the category of caesarean section
blocks.prompt: Case A: a woman in labour has a sustained fetal bradycardia of 60 beats per minute for 8 minutes. Case B: a woman at 41 weeks has failure to progress at 6 cm with a normal CTG and a stable condition. Classify each and state the aim for the decision-to-delivery interval.

steps.text: Case A: a persistent profound bradycardia suggests acute fetal hypoxia, an immediate threat to the life of the fetus. This is Category 1.
The standard for Category 1 is delivery as quickly as possible, usually within 30 minutes of decision, and in an emergency theatre team activation.

Case B: arrested progress without maternal or fetal compromise, but needing early delivery, is Category 3 (some units class this as Category 2 if there are concerns). A decision interval of hours is acceptable and the woman can be counselled and consented at leisure.

blocks.answer: Case A is Category 1 (delivery within about 30 minutes); Case B is Category 3.

blocks.markdown: **Shoulder dystocia** is when, after delivery of the head, the anterior shoulder is trapped behind the pubic symphysis and routine downward traction fails. Risk factors include fetal macrosomia, maternal diabetes, previous shoulder dystocia, high maternal BMI, prolonged labour and instrumental delivery, although most cases are unpredicted. The 'turtle sign' (head retracting against the perineum) is a clue. Complications include brachial plexus injury (for example Erb's palsy from C5 and C6 injury), clavicular or humeral fracture, hypoxic injury, postpartum haemorrhage and perineal tears. The management follows the **HELPERR** mnemonic, used in UK practice: call for **Help**, **Evaluate** for episiotomy, **Legs** (McRoberts position: hyperflexion and abduction of the maternal hips), suprapubic **Pressure** applied from the side of the fetal back, **Enter** manoeuvres (internal rotation), **Remove** the posterior arm and **Roll** the woman onto all fours. Do not apply fundal pressure, and avoid excessive traction.

**Cord prolapse** occurs when the umbilical cord descends below the presenting part after membrane rupture. It is associated with malpresentation, prematurity, polyhydramnios, a high or unengaged head and artificial rupture of membranes. Compression and vasospasm of the cord cut off fetal oxygen supply. Diagnosis is by palpating the cord on vaginal examination or seeing it at the introitus, often after a fetal bradycardia. Management: call for help, **move the woman into knee-chest or exaggerated left lateral position with head down**, **manually elevate the presenting part** (a finger in the vagina keeps it off the cord), handle the cord as little as possible and do not push it back, consider bladder filling with about 500 mL saline, consider tocolysis, and arrange immediate delivery, normally a Category 1 caesarean section unless vaginal birth is quicker and safer.

items: Delay is diagnosed from progress across the labour, not from a single exam.
Powers are the most correctable cause; weak contractions respond to amniotomy and oxytocin.
Instrumental birth needs full dilatation, an engaged head and a known position.
Shoulder dystocia is a call-for-help emergency managed by HELPERR.
Cord prolapse is relieved by elevating the presenting part and expediting delivery.

blocks.title: Intervene on the trend and the fetus
blocks.text: Time thresholds identify delay, but the choice to intervene rests on maternal condition, fetal heart rate pattern and the likely cause. The faster the fetal condition deteriorates, the more urgent the category of delivery.

points: Failure to progress is analysed as problems of powers, passage or passenger; amniotomy and oxytocin treat inadequate contractions when there is no obstruction.
Instrumental delivery needs fully dilated cervix, ruptured membranes, engaged head with known position, empty bladder, analgesia and a back-up plan.
Caesarean section is graded Category 1 to 4 by urgency, with Category 1 aiming for delivery within 30 minutes.
Shoulder dystocia follows HELPERR without fundal pressure; cord prolapse is managed by elevating the presenting part and urgent delivery.

questions.stem: A nulliparous woman at term was found to be 4 cm dilated with regular contractions and intact membranes. Four hours later she is 5 cm. Contractions are 2 in 10 minutes and the fetal heart rate is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Immediate Category 1 caesarean section
Artificial rupture of the membranes, with an oxytocin infusion if progress remains inadequate
Wait a further 8 hours before reassessment
Forceps delivery

questions.correctOptionText: Artificial rupture of the membranes, with an oxytocin infusion if progress remains inadequate

distractorRationale.a: There is no fetal or maternal compromise to justify immediate surgery.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: dilatation of 1 cm in 4 hours is less than the 2 cm threshold and the contractions are weak, so correct the powers.
distractorRationale.c: Waiting without intervention ignores established delay.
distractorRationale.d: She is not fully dilated; forceps are contraindicated.

questions.explanation: Progress of 1 cm in 4 hours is less than 2 cm, which defines delay in the established first stage. With only two contractions in 10 minutes the likely cause is inadequate powers, so amniotomy followed by oxytocin is the first correction.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a required prerequisite for a forceps or ventouse delivery?

options.text: Cervix at least 8 cm dilated
Intact membranes
Fully dilated cervix with a known position of the fetal head
Fetal head floating above the pelvic brim

questions.correctOptionText: Fully dilated cervix with a known position of the fetal head

distractorRationale.a: Application through a partly dilated cervix risks cervical laceration.
distractorRationale.b: Membranes must be ruptured so the instrument can be applied to the fetal head.
distractorRationale.d: The head must be engaged, with no more than one-fifth palpable abdominally.

questions.explanation: Instruments are applied only when the cervix is fully dilated and the exact position of the head is known so that the application and direction of traction are correct. An unengaged head or partial dilatation makes the attempt dangerous.

questions.stem: After the fetal head delivers, it retracts firmly against the perineum and routine downward traction fails to deliver the anterior shoulder. After calling for help, which is the most appropriate first manoeuvre?

options.text: Fundal pressure
McRoberts position with suprapubic pressure
Strong downward and lateral traction on the head
Immediate symphysiotomy

distractorRationale.a: Fundal pressure drives the shoulder further against the symphysis and is contraindicated.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: hip hyperflexion and suprapubic pressure are the first manoeuvres in the HELPERR sequence.
distractorRationale.c: Excessive traction risks brachial plexus injury.
distractorRationale.d: Symphysiotomy is a last resort and not a first-line manoeuvre.

questions.explanation: The turtle sign and failed traction diagnose shoulder dystocia. McRoberts position straightens the sacral angle and rotates the symphysis, and suprapubic pressure adducts the shoulders, resolving most cases without further manoeuvres.

questions.stem: A woman at 34 weeks with polyhydramnios has artificial rupture of membranes and a cord loop is felt below the presenting part. The fetal heart rate is 90 beats per minute. She is 5 cm dilated. Which management is correct?

options.text: Replace the cord into the uterus and continue labour
Elevate the presenting part manually, place her knee-chest or head down, and arrange an immediate Category 1 caesarean section
Start an oxytocin infusion to speed delivery
Wait and observe for 30 minutes

questions.correctOptionText: Elevate the presenting part manually, place her knee-chest or head down, and arrange an immediate Category 1 caesarean section

distractorRationale.a: Replacing the cord risks further compression and is not recommended.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: relieve cord compression and expedite delivery, as she is not fully dilated.
distractorRationale.c: Oxytocin increases compression and does not avoid delay.
distractorRationale.d: Delay in a bradycardic fetus risks hypoxic injury.

questions.explanation: Cord prolapse with fetal bradycardia is an obstetric emergency and the cord must be protected from compression while delivery is arranged. Because she is only 5 cm dilated, caesarean section is the quickest safe route.

questions.stem: A woman in labour has a normal CTG but obstructed labour confirmed at 8 cm dilatation with a deflexed occipito-posterior head and significant caput and moulding. She is clinically well. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Oxytocin augmentation should be started because the powers are inadequate
Attempt rotational forceps now at 8 cm
Caesarean section is indicated because obstruction is a mechanical problem that oxytocin will not correct
Continue to wait for 8 hours

questions.correctOptionText: Caesarean section is indicated because obstruction is a mechanical problem that oxytocin will not correct

distractorRationale.a: Oxytocin against an obstruction risks uterine rupture.
distractorRationale.b: The cervix must be fully dilated for any instrumental delivery.
distractorRationale.d: Waiting leads to uterine rupture and fetal compromise.

questions.explanation: Caput and moulding with a deflexed occipito-posterior head at 8 cm indicate disproportion, a problem of passenger and passage, not of the powers. Augmenting contractions against obstruction can rupture the uterus, so caesarean section is the safe route.

questions.stem: True or false: A ventouse (vacuum extractor) is the preferred instrument for a preterm fetus of 30 weeks gestation.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The ventouse is avoided before 34 weeks and is contraindicated below 32 weeks because the preterm skull and fragile vessels are at risk of intracranial and subgaleal haemorrhage. Forceps are the instrument of choice in this situation when instrumental delivery is needed.

questions.stem: Oxytocin 30 units is made up in 500 mL of crystalloid and infused at 10 mL per hour (teaching example only). Calculate the dose being delivered in milliunits per minute (mU/min).
questions.explanation: The concentration is 30 000 mU divided by 500 mL, which is 60 mU per mL. At 10 mL per hour the rate is 600 mU per hour, or 10 mU per minute.

questions.stem: A Category 1 caesarean section is decided at 02:14 after a prolonged fetal bradycardia, and the baby is delivered at 02:51. Calculate the decision-to-delivery interval in minutes.
questions.explanation: From 02:14 to 02:51 is 37 minutes. This is longer than the 30-minute aim for Category 1 delivery, so the team should audit the delay.

questions.stem: A nulliparous woman has been pushing for 2 hours at full dilatation with no descent of the head beyond the ischial spines. Discuss the possible causes and your assessment and management, including when you would consider instrumental delivery or caesarean section.
markingGuide: Causes framed as powers, passage and passenger (weak contractions or epidural, pelvic or soft-tissue obstruction, malposition such as occipito-posterior or macrosomia)
Assessment: abdominal and vaginal examination, position, caput, moulding, bladder, fetal heart rate and maternal condition
Delay in second stage in a nulliparous woman defined as about 2 hours of active second stage, needing obstetric review
Correct powers with oxytocin if contractions are inadequate and there is no obstruction
Instrumental delivery only if prerequisites met: full dilatation, ruptured membranes, engaged head with known position, empty bladder, analgesia, consent and back-up plan
Caesarean section if head high, malposition not correctable, obstruction or fetal compromise
questions.explanation: A lack of descent is analysed through the three Ps. Management is matched to the cause, and instrumental delivery is reserved for cases that meet the prerequisites; otherwise caesarean section avoids trauma.

questions.stem: Describe the immediate management of shoulder dystocia, listing the manoeuvres in order and the actions that should be avoided, and state two serious neonatal complications.
markingGuide: Call for help including neonatal team and note the time
Do not apply fundal pressure and avoid excessive traction on the head
McRoberts position (hyperflexion and abduction of maternal hips)
Suprapubic pressure from the side of the fetal back
Consider episiotomy to allow internal access
Internal manoeuvres (rotational) and delivery of the posterior arm
Roll to all fours if still undelivered
Complications: brachial plexus injury, clavicle or humerus fracture, hypoxic injury
Careful documentation and review for postpartum haemorrhage and perineal trauma
questions.explanation: Shoulder dystocia is managed by an ordered series of manoeuvres that increase pelvic space or reduce the shoulder diameter. Fundal pressure and strong traction worsen impaction and injure the brachial plexus.
